chapters.title: Counting steps (Big-O and reading the limits)
chapters.tagline: Before you write a line, the input size tells you which algorithm is allowed
goals: Count how many steps a loop takes, as a function of n
Name the common growth rates: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², 2ⁿ
Read a problem's limits and know the slowest solution that still passes
Replace a double loop with one pass, using a little maths
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    """Run fn(*args) and return (result, seconds)."""
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
Two correct programs can differ by a factor of a million in speed. Timing them on your laptop with 10 items tells you nothing: both finish instantly. What matters is how the work grows when the input gets bigger. That's what Big-O describes: drop the constants, keep the shape.

A computer does roughly 10⁸ simple steps a second (pure Python is slower, nearer 10⁷). Every problem on LeetCode or Codeforces states its limits, like 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 000, and a time limit of 1 or 2 seconds. Put those together and you know what kind of solution the setter expects before you've read the rest.

blocks.name: ds-bigo
blocks.title: How fast each kind of algorithm grows
blocks.goal: Solve all three puzzles: for each limit on n, pick the most work you can afford in about a second.
blocks.intro: Click any bar to see an example of that kind of algorithm and how long it would take.

blocks.html: Count how many times the innermost line runs. A loop over range(n) runs n times; a loop inside a loop multiplies.
Every pair (i, j) with i < j is counted once: n(n−1)/2 pairs. That's about n²/2, and Big-O drops the ½: it's O(n²).

blocks.q: How many times does the loop body run, as a function of n? while n > 1: n = n // 2
blocks.why: Each step halves n. Starting from a million, you reach 1 after about 20 halvings, because 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶. Halving is the signature of O(log n).

blocks.q: for i in range(n): for j in range(0, n, 2): ... What's the Big-O?

opts.t: O(n² / 2), which is different from O(n²)

blocks.why: The inner loop runs n/2 times for each of n values of i: n²/2 steps. Constant factors like ½ are dropped, so it's O(n²). (They still matter in practice, but they never change which bar you're on.)

blocks.q: for i in range(n): j = 1; while j < n: j *= 2. What's the Big-O?
blocks.why: The outer loop runs n times; the inner one doubles j, so it runs about log₂ n times. n × log n.

sections.title: One pass instead of two loops

blocks.html: The most common speed-up in all of DSA: instead of looking back at every earlier item, remember a summary of what you've seen so far (the smallest, the sum, the count). Then each new item costs O(1).

blocks.title: best_profit
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. prices[i] is a share's price on day i. You may buy on one day and sell on a later day, once. Write best_profit(prices) returning the most money you can make (0 if every choice loses money). n can be 200 000, so trying every pair (buy day, sell day) is too slow.
blocks.tests:
assert best_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]) == 5, "buy at 1, sell at 6"
assert best_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1]) == 0, "prices only fall: don't trade"
assert best_profit([2]) == 0
assert best_profit([3, 3, 3]) == 0
assert best_profit([1, 9, 0, 5]) == 8, "the later low (0) doesn't beat 9 - 1"
big = list(range(5000, 0, -1))
r, secs = timed(best_profit, big)
assert r == 0
assert secs < 0.25, f"took {secs:.2f}s on 5 000 days: that's the O(n²) double loop. Keep the lowest price so far instead."
hints: On each day, the best sale is today's price minus the lowest price before today. Keep that lowest price in a variable as you walk.
Two variables, one loop: lowest = min(lowest, p) and best = max(best, p - lowest).
blocks.solution:
def best_profit(prices):
    lowest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best

blocks.title: The largest and second-largest in one pass

blocks.html: The decoys show the trap: when a new maximum arrives, the old maximum becomes second. Overwrite first before saving it and it's gone.

blocks.title: missing_number
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. nums holds n different numbers from 0..n, so exactly one number in that range is missing. Return it, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (no set, no sorting).
blocks.tests:
assert missing_number([3, 0, 1]) == 2
assert missing_number([0, 1]) == 2
assert missing_number([1]) == 0
assert missing_number([9, 6, 4, 2, 3, 5, 7, 0, 1]) == 8
big = list(range(20000)); big.remove(12345)
r, secs = timed(missing_number, big)
assert r == 12345
assert secs < 0.2, f"{secs:.2f}s: `k not in nums` scans the whole list each time, so this is O(n²)"
hints: 0 + 1 + … + n = n(n+1)/2. The total of what's there is sum(nums). The difference is the missing number.

blocks.html: k not in nums looks like one step but it's a hidden loop over the list. Spotting hidden loops (in on a list, list.index, list.remove, slicing, string += in a loop) is half of Big-O in Python.

blocks.q: Which of these is not O(1) in Python?
blocks.why: in on a list checks items one by one: O(n). On a set or dict it's O(1) on average, because they hash. That's the whole of chapter 3.

blocks.title: pair_products
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. Given a list a of up to 2·10⁵ integers, return the sum of a[i] * a[j] over all pairs i < j. The double loop is 2·10¹⁰ steps. Find an O(n) way.
blocks.tests:
assert pair_products([1, 2, 3]) == 1*2 + 1*3 + 2*3
assert pair_products([5]) == 0
assert pair_products([]) == 0
assert pair_products([-1, 4, 2, -3]) == -4 - 2 + 3 + 8 - 12 - 6
big = list(range(1, 4001))
r, secs = timed(pair_products, big)
s = sum(big); assert r == (s * s - sum(x * x for x in big)) // 2
assert secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: too slow, that's the O(n²) double loop"
hints: Each x gets multiplied by every number before it. That's x * (sum of the earlier numbers). Keep the running sum.
Another route: (a₁ + … + aₙ)² = Σaᵢ² + 2·Σ_{i<j} aᵢaⱼ, so the answer is (sum(a)**2 - sum of squares) // 2.
blocks.solution:
def pair_products(a):
    total = 0
    seen = 0
    for x in a:
        total += x * seen
        seen += x
    return total

blocks.code:
calls = 0
def f(n):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    if n > 1:
        f(n // 2)
        f(n // 2)
f(16)
print(calls)

blocks.html: Each call makes two calls on half the size. The levels have 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 calls: 31 in total, about 2n. Not every recursion is slow; it depends how fast the problem shrinks. (Chapter 5 builds this from scratch.)

blocks.q: A problem: "1 ≤ n ≤ 18. Choose some of the n items so their weights sum to exactly W." What does the limit tell you?

opts.t: Trying every subset is allowed: 2¹⁸ ≈ 260 000 subsets

blocks.why: n ≤ 20 is the setter saying "brute force over subsets is fine." Small limits are a hint, not an accident.

blocks.title: A "will it scale?" checker for a team's code
blocks.client: A start-up whose search page was fast in testing and timed out on launch day with 50 000 users
blocks.brief: Build scale.py that takes a function and an input generator, runs the function at sizes n = 1 000, 2 000, 4 000, 8 000, … (stopping when one run takes more than 2 seconds), and reports the growth: "looks like O(n²): at your production size of 50 000 this takes about 40 s". Fit the slope of log(time) against log(n): a slope near 1 is linear, near 2 quadratic. Add it to the test suite so a slow change fails the build.
blocks.why: Performance bugs pass every functional test and only show up at real sizes. Doubling the input and watching the time is how engineers spot O(n²) before users do; the same idea (benchmarks in CI) runs at every large tech company.

Estimate the exponent from the timings
Predict the time at a production size
Fail loudly when the exponent jumps between two versions
stretch: Repeat each timing a few times and take the minimum (noise only ever makes things slower)
Tell n log n apart from n (it needs a wider range of sizes)

blocks.title: growth_exponent
blocks.prompt: Write growth_exponent(sizes, seconds): given input sizes and how long each run took, return the slope of the best straight line through the points (log n, log t) (least squares), rounded to 1 decimal. A slope of 2.0 means time grows like n².
hints: On a log-log plot, t = c·nᵏ is a straight line with slope k. Least-squares slope: Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / Σ(x−x̄)².
blocks.solution:
import math

def growth_exponent(sizes, seconds):
    xs = [math.log(n) for n in sizes]
    ys = [math.log(t) for t in seconds]
    mx, my = sum(xs) / len(xs), sum(ys) / len(ys)
    slope = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x in xs)
    return round(slope, 1)

blocks.title: predict_time
blocks.prompt: Write predict_time(n0, t0, k, n): a run at size n0 took t0 seconds and time grows like nᵏ. Return the predicted seconds at size n, rounded to 2 decimals.
blocks.tests:
assert predict_time(8000, 0.64, 2, 50000) == 25.0
assert predict_time(1000, 0.5, 1, 4000) == 2.0
assert predict_time(100, 0.01, 3, 1000) == 10.0
hints: Ten times the input with k = 2 is a hundred times the time: t0 * (n / n0) ** k.
blocks.starter:
def predict_time(n0, t0, k, n):
    return t0
blocks.solution:
def predict_time(n0, t0, k, n):
    return round(t0 * (n / n0) ** k, 2)

blocks.q: s = "" then for w in words: s += w. In the worst case, what can this cost for n words?

opts.t: O(n²) characters copied, because strings can't be changed in place

blocks.why: Each += may build a brand-new string and copy everything so far. "".join(words) copies each character once: O(total length).

blocks.q: An O(n²) solution takes 1 second at n = 10 000. About how long at n = 100 000?
blocks.why: 10× the input, squared: 100× the time. Doubling n doubles an O(n) program and quadruples an O(n²) one.

blocks.q: Which grows fastest as n gets large?
blocks.why: Any exponential beats any polynomial in the end. 2ⁿ passes n¹⁰ at about n = 59 and never looks back.

blocks.q: a.sort() followed by one loop over a. Total?
blocks.why: Add the steps: n log n + n. Keep only the biggest term: O(n log n).

blocks.q: for i in range(n): if i in seen_set: ... where seen_set is a Python set. Total?
blocks.why: A set lookup is O(1) on average (it hashes), so n lookups cost O(n). With a list instead of a set, the same line would be O(n²).

blocks.q: A problem allows n ≤ 10¹⁸. What kind of solution is it asking for?

opts.t: A formula, or something that halves (O(log n)) like binary search or fast power

blocks.why: You can't even loop to 10¹⁸. The answer must come from maths or from cutting the problem in half each step.

blocks.title: allowed_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: allowed(n) returns the most work you can afford for that n: "n!" up to 10, "2^n" up to 20, "n^3" up to 500, "n^2" up to 5 000, "n log n" up to 10⁶, "n" up to 10⁸, else "log n".
hints: Seven if lines, smallest limit first.
blocks.starter:
def allowed(n):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def allowed(n):
    if n <= 10: return "n!"
    if n <= 20: return "2^n"
    if n <= 500: return "n^3"
    if n <= 5000: return "n^2"
    if n <= 10**6: return "n log n"
    if n <= 10**8: return "n"
    return "log n"

blocks.q: What does Big-O measure, and how do you use a problem's limits to choose an algorithm?
blocks.a: Big-O describes how the number of steps grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors: a loop over n items is O(n), two nested loops over all pairs O(n²), halving each step O(log n), trying every subset O(2ⁿ). A computer does roughly 10⁸ simple steps a second (pure Python closer to 10⁷), so the limit on n tells you the most work you can afford: n ≤ 20 allows 2ⁿ, n ≤ 5 000 allows n², n up to about 10⁶ needs n log n or better, and huge n needs O(log n) maths. To speed something up, keep a running summary (lowest so far, running sum) instead of looking back at every earlier item, and watch for hidden loops like x in list.

chapters.title: Arrays in one pass
chapters.tagline: Keep a small summary as you walk, and swap in place instead of building new lists
goals: Find the maximum-sum stretch of an array in one pass (Kadane)
Use a write pointer to filter an array in place
Rotate and reverse in place with O(1) extra memory
Sort three kinds of value in one pass (the Dutch flag)
chapters.prelude:
import time, random

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
An array is a row of boxes in memory, side by side. Reading a[i] is instant because the computer jumps straight to box i. Most array problems are about walking that row once while carrying a few numbers in your head.

The classic: which stretch of neighbouring numbers (a subarray) has the largest total? Think of a shop's profit and loss per day, and the best run of days to show investors.

blocks.name: ds-kadane
blocks.title: Every stretch, or one walk
blocks.goal: Run try every stretch to the end, then run Kadane to the end and compare how many stretches each looked at.
blocks.intro: Click any number to see why it helps or hurts a stretch.

blocks.html: The idea in one sentence: if the run you're carrying has a negative total, drop it, because adding a negative start to anything only makes it smaller.

blocks.code:
a = [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]
run = 0
for x in a:
    run = max(x, run + x)
    print(run, end=" ")

blocks.html: run = max(x, run + x) is the same rule written another way: either extend the run with x, or start fresh at x, whichever is bigger. The answer is the largest run ever seen (6, for 4 -1 2 1).

blocks.title: Kadane's algorithm
blocks.tests:
assert max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]) == 6
assert max_subarray([-3, -1, -2]) == -1
assert max_subarray([5]) == 5

blocks.html: The first decoy is the classic bug: starting best at 0 gives the wrong answer when every number is negative (the best stretch is then the single largest number, not an empty one).

blocks.q: a = [-3, -1, -2]. What should max_subarray(a) return if a stretch must contain at least one number?
blocks.why: The best you can do is the single number -1. A version that starts best = 0 returns 0, which is only right if empty stretches are allowed. Always check the all-negative case.

blocks.title: max_subarray_where
blocks.prompt: An interview classic, one step harder. Write best_stretch(a) returning (total, start, end) for the maximum-sum subarray (inclusive indices). If several stretches tie, return the one that starts earliest, and among those the shortest. a has at least one number and can have 10⁵ of them.
blocks.tests:
assert best_stretch([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]) == (6, 3, 6)
assert best_stretch([-3, -1, -2]) == (-1, 1, 1)
assert best_stretch([2, -2, 2]) == (2, 0, 0), "ties: earliest start, then shortest"
assert best_stretch([1, 2, 3]) == (6, 0, 2)
big = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(5000)]
r, secs = timed(best_stretch, big)
assert r[0] == sum(big[r[1]:r[2] + 1])
assert secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: too slow, use one walk"
hints: Carry run and the index start where the current run began. When run is negative, reset run = 0 and start = j before adding a[j].
Only replace best when the new total is strictly bigger: that keeps the earliest, shortest one on ties.
blocks.starter:
def best_stretch(a):
    return (0, 0, 0)

sections.title: Filtering in place: the write pointer

blocks.html: Building a new list costs memory. Many interview questions say "do it in place". The pattern: one index reads every item, another (w, the write pointer) marks where the next kept item goes.

blocks.title: move_zeroes
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. Move every 0 in the list a to the end, in place, keeping the other numbers in their original order. Return nothing; change a itself.
blocks.tests:
a = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]; move_zeroes(a); assert a == [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]
a = [0]; move_zeroes(a); assert a == [0]
a = [4, 2]; move_zeroes(a); assert a == [4, 2]
a = [0, 5, 0]; b = a; r = move_zeroes(a); assert b == [5, 0, 0] and r is None, "change the list itself, don't return a new one"
hints: Walk with x. Every non-zero goes to a[w], then w += 1. Afterwards, fill from w to the end with zeros.
blocks.starter:
def move_zeroes(a):
    return [x for x in a if x != 0] + [0] * a.count(0)

blocks.title: dedupe_sorted
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. a is sorted. Remove duplicates in place so the first k slots hold each distinct value once, in order, and return k. (What's after slot k doesn't matter.)
blocks.tests:
a = [1, 1, 2]; k = dedupe_sorted(a); assert k == 2 and a[:k] == [1, 2]
a = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]; k = dedupe_sorted(a); assert k == 5 and a[:k] == [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
a = []; assert dedupe_sorted(a) == 0
a = [7]; assert dedupe_sorted(a) == 1 and a == [7]
hints: Because it's sorted, a duplicate always sits right after its twin. Compare a[i] with the last value you kept, a[w - 1].
blocks.starter:
def dedupe_sorted(a):
    return len(set(a))

blocks.code:
def reverse(a, lo, hi):
    while lo < hi:
        a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
        lo += 1
        hi -= 1

a = list("ABCDEFG")
reverse(a, 0, len(a) - 1)
print("".join(a))
blocks.title: Reverse with two pointers

blocks.html: Rotating right by k (the last k items move to the front) looks like it needs a second list. It doesn't: reverse the whole thing, then reverse the first k, then reverse the rest.

blocks.code:
a = list("ABCDEFG")
k = 3
def rev(lo, hi):
    while lo < hi:
        a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
        lo, hi = lo + 1, hi - 1
rev(0, 6); print("".join(a))
rev(0, k - 1); print("".join(a))
rev(k, 6); print("".join(a))

blocks.title: rotate_bug
blocks.prompt: This rotation works for small k but crashes or gives the wrong answer when k is bigger than the list (rotating 7 items by 10 is the same as rotating by 3), and when the list is empty. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
a = list("ABCDEFG"); rotate(a, 3); assert "".join(a) == "EFGABCD"
a = list("ABCDEFG"); rotate(a, 10); assert "".join(a) == "EFGABCD", "10 steps on 7 items = 3 steps"
a = list("ABC"); rotate(a, 3); assert "".join(a) == "ABC"
a = []; rotate(a, 5); assert a == []
hints: Rotating by n changes nothing, so only k % n matters. Guard the empty list first (% 0 would crash).

sections.title: Three kinds in one pass: the Dutch flag

blocks.html: Sort a list holding only 0s, 1s and 2s, in one pass, in place. Keep three regions: everything before lo is 0, everything after hi is 2, and mid walks the unknown part in between.

blocks.title: Dutch national flag
blocks.tests:
a = [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]; sort_colors(a); assert a == [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
a = [2, 2, 0]; sort_colors(a); assert a == [0, 2, 2]
a = []; sort_colors(a); assert a == []
a = [1]; sort_colors(a); assert a == [1]

blocks.q: In the Dutch flag, after swapping a[mid] with a[hi], why don't we move mid forward?

opts.t: The number that came from hi hasn't been looked at yet, so mid must check it
To keep the loop running longer

blocks.why: Everything after hi was unknown. The swap brings one of those unknowns to mid, and it could be a 0, 1 or 2. (After a swap with lo it's safe to move on: that slot was already checked.)

blocks.title: make_non_decreasing
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. In one operation you may add 1 to any element. Return the minimum number of operations to make a non-decreasing (each element ≥ the one before it). n up to 2·10⁵, values up to 10⁹.
blocks.tests:

assert make_non_decreasing([1, 2, 3]) == 0
assert make_non_decreasing([5, 4, 3, 2, 1]) == 1 + 2 + 3 + 4
assert make_non_decreasing([10**9, 1]) == 10**9 - 1
assert make_non_decreasing([]) == 0
hints: Raising an element to exactly the largest value so far is always enough and never wasteful. Carry that running maximum.

blocks.title: max_product
blocks.prompt: An interview favourite that breaks Kadane. Return the largest product of a non-empty stretch of a (integers, may be negative or zero). A negative times a negative is positive, so the smallest product so far matters too.
blocks.tests:
assert max_product([2, 3, -2, 4]) == 6
assert max_product([-2, 0, -1]) == 0
assert max_product([-2, 3, -4]) == 24, "two negatives make a positive"
assert max_product([-2]) == -2
assert max_product([0, 2]) == 2
hints: Carry two runs: the biggest and the smallest product ending here. A negative x turns the smallest into the biggest.
blocks.solution:
def max_product(a):
    best = hi = lo = a[0]
    for x in a[1:]:
        cands = (x, hi * x, lo * x)
        hi, lo = max(cands), min(cands)
        best = max(best, hi)
    return best

blocks.title: leaders
blocks.prompt: A warm-up that teaches walking backwards. An element is a leader if it's strictly greater than everything to its right (the last element always is). Return the leaders in their original left-to-right order, in O(n).
blocks.tests:
assert leaders([16, 17, 4, 3, 5, 2]) == [17, 5, 2]
assert leaders([1, 2, 3]) == [3]
assert leaders([]) == []
big = list(range(6000, 0, -1))
r, secs = timed(leaders, big)
assert r == big and secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: walk from the right, keeping the maximum seen"
hints: From the right, "greater than everything to my right" means "greater than the maximum so far".
blocks.starter:
def leaders(a):
    return [x for i, x in enumerate(a) if all(x > y for y in a[i + 1:])]

blocks.q: What does Kadane's algorithm throw away, and when?

opts.t: The smallest number, at the end
The current run, as soon as its total is negative
The best answer, when a bigger one appears

blocks.why: A run with a negative total can only lower whatever follows, so starting fresh is never worse.

blocks.q: What's the extra memory used by the write-pointer filter?

opts.t: O(k), for the k items kept

blocks.why: It overwrites the same list. That's what "in place" means.

blocks.q: Rotating 1 000 items right by 1 000 003 steps. How many steps actually matter?
blocks.why: Every 1 000 steps brings the list back to where it started: 1 000 003 % 1 000 = 3.

blocks.q: Which problem is not a "carry one summary while walking" problem?

opts.t: Best day to buy and sell a share
Counting how many pairs of equal numbers there are, without extra memory and in O(n), when the numbers are unsorted

blocks.why: The first three each need just one or two running numbers. Counting equal pairs in unsorted data needs to remember which values you've seen: that's a hash map (chapter 3), or sorting first.

sections.title: Real-world project: the best run of days

blocks.title: A "best run" report for a small business
blocks.client: A café owner with three years of daily profit and loss in a spreadsheet, preparing to talk to the bank
blocks.brief: Build bestrun.py daily.csv that prints the best stretch of consecutive days (total, start date, end date), the worst stretch (the deepest loss), and the longest streak of profitable days. Then handle the café's question about the yearly cycle: treat the year as a circle (December wraps into January) and find the best stretch on that circle.
blocks.why: "Best and worst consecutive periods" appear in finance (maximum drawdown), monitoring (longest outage), genomics (high-scoring DNA segments) and sport (best scoring run). Kadane is the engine behind all of them.

Worst stretch (the same algorithm, flipped)
Longest run of profitable days
Best stretch when the year wraps around
stretch: Report the best stretch of at least 7 days

blocks.q: Explain Kadane's algorithm and the write-pointer pattern, and why each is O(n).
blocks.a: Kadane walks the array once, carrying run = the best total of a stretch ending at the current element. For each x, run = max(x, run + x): extend the stretch, or start fresh if the old run was negative and could only drag things down. The answer is the largest run seen. Starting best at a[0], not 0, handles all-negative arrays. The write pointer filters in place: one index reads every element, w marks where the next kept element goes, so nothing is copied to a new list and extra memory is O(1). Both touch every element a constant number of times, so they're O(n), versus O(n²) for trying every start and end. Related in-place tricks: reverse with two pointers, rotate by k with three reversals (k % n), and the Dutch flag with three regions lo/mid/hi.

blocks.q: A hash table's lookup is O(1) on average. When can it be O(n)?

blocks.q: You need "pairs with a[i] + i == a[j] - j". What's the key trick?

blocks.q: How does a hash table give O(1) lookups, and what's the two-sum pattern?
blocks.a: A hash table computes a hash number from the key and uses it to choose a bucket, then only compares against the few keys in that bucket. With a good hash function and a table that grows as it fills, buckets stay tiny, so lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average (O(n) in the worst case, if everything collides). Keys must be immutable, because the bucket is chosen from the hash when the key is stored. The two-sum pattern: walk the array once; for each x, ask whether its partner (target − x) has been seen, then store x. Storing counts instead of indices counts pairs. More generally, rewrite a pair condition so one side depends only on i and the other only on j (for example a[i] − i == a[j] − j), then count with a dict as you walk: O(n) instead of O(n²).

blocks.html:
A shop has ten years of daily sales, and the manager keeps asking: "what did we sell between day 1 200 and day 1 450?" Adding up the range each time is slow when there are many questions. Instead, build the running total once: P[k] = the sum of the first k days. Then

because everything up to day r, minus everything before day l, leaves exactly the days in between.

def subarray_sum_k(a, k):
    seen = Counter({0: 1})
    run = count = 0
    for x in a:
        run += x
        count += seen[run - k]
        seen[run] += 1
    return count

def divisible_subarrays(a, k):
    seen = Counter({0: 1})
    run = count = 0
    for x in a:
        run = (run + x) % k
        count += seen[run]
        seen[run] += 1
    return count

blocks.solution:
def product_except_self(a):
    n = len(a)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= a[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= a[i]
    return out

blocks.q: "Count subarrays with sum exactly k" when numbers can be negative. Which tool?

blocks.q: A difference array update "add 5 to positions 3..8" changes how many entries of D?

blocks.q: Prefix sums need the array to stay fixed. What if values change between queries?

blocks.q: Explain prefix sums, the prefix-sum + hash-map trick, and difference arrays.
blocks.a: A prefix array P has P[0] = 0 and P[k] = a[0] + … + a[k-1]. Building it is O(n); then any range sum a[l..r] = P[r+1] − P[l] in O(1), because the total up to r minus the total before l leaves just the range. The leading zero removes edge cases. To count subarrays summing to k, note that l..r works exactly when P[l] = P[r+1] − k, so walk once keeping a dict of how many times each prefix sum has appeared (starting {0: 1}) and add the count of run − k at each step: two-sum on prefix sums, which works with negative numbers. Equal remainders mod k give subarrays divisible by k. A difference array does the opposite: to add v to a[l..r], do D[l] += v and D[r+1] −= v; one prefix sum at the end applies every update, so u updates cost O(u + n). In 2D, S[i+1][j+1] = grid[i][j] + above + left − above-left, and a rectangle is four lookups by inclusion-exclusion.

chapters.title: Recursion and the call stack
chapters.tagline: Solve a problem by trusting a smaller copy of it, and remember answers you've already found
goals: Write a recursive function with a base case and a smaller step
Trace the call stack and predict the order things happen
Spot repeated work and remove it with a memo
Turn deep recursion into a loop when the stack would overflow
chapters.prelude:
import sys, time
from functools import lru_cache

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version, and has a base case small enough to answer directly. The leap of faith: while writing fact(n) = n * fact(n - 1), assume fact(n - 1) already works.

Underneath, each call gets a frame on the call stack (its own n, its own local variables, and where to return to). A call can't finish until the calls it made have finished, so frames pile up and then unwind.

blocks.name: ds-recur
blocks.title: The call tree and the call stack of fib(6)

blocks.intro: Step slowly at first: watch the stack on the right grow as calls start, and shrink as they return.

blocks.code:
def fact(n, depth=0):
    print("  " * depth + f"fact({n}) starts")
    result = 1 if n <= 1 else n * fact(n - 1, depth + 1)
    print("  " * depth + f"fact({n}) returns {result}")
    return result

fact(4)
blocks.title: Watching frames open and close

blocks.code:
def show(n):
    if n == 0:
        return
    print("before", n)
    show(n - 1)
    print("after", n)

show(3)

blocks.html: Everything before the recursive call happens on the way down (3, 2, 1); everything after it happens on the way back up, in reverse (1, 2, 3). That's how the stack lets recursion "remember" where it was.

blocks.q: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?

opts.t: It loops forever, using no extra memory
Each call opens a new frame until Python's limit (about 1 000) and raises RecursionError
Python detects it and stops at the first call

blocks.why: Frames take memory, so infinite recursion runs out of stack. Python sets a limit (sys.getrecursionlimit()) to fail cleanly instead of crashing.

sections.title: When the stack is too deep

blocks.html: Python's stack holds about 1 000 frames. A recursion that goes n levels deep fails at n = 10⁵, even with a memo. Contest solutions in Python usually turn such recursions into loops: compute small answers first and build up. That's a bottom-up table, the other face of dynamic programming.

blocks.title: ways_134
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. Count the ways to write n as an ordered sum of 1s, 3s and 4s (so 1+3 and 3+1 are different), modulo 1 000 000 007. n up to 10⁵, so recursion would overflow the stack: build the answers from 0 upwards in a list.
blocks.tests:

assert ways(3) == 2, "1+1+1, 3"
assert ways(4) == 4, "1+1+1+1, 1+3, 3+1, 4"
assert ways(5) == 6
r, secs = timed(ways, 100000)
assert secs < 0.5 and 0 <= r < 1_000_000_007
hints: w[i] = w[i-1] + w[i-3] + w[i-4] (skipping negative indices), starting from w[0] = 1 (one way to make 0: take nothing).
blocks.solution:
def ways(n):
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    w = [0] * (n + 1)
    w[0] = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        w[i] = (w[i - 1] + (w[i - 3] if i >= 3 else 0) + (w[i - 4] if i >= 4 else 0)) % MOD
    return w[n]

blocks.q: How many frames are on the stack at the deepest point of fact(5)?
blocks.why: fact(5) waits for fact(4), which waits for fact(3)… down to fact(1): five frames at once. Stack depth = depth of the recursion, not the number of calls.

blocks.q: Plain recursive fib(n) makes about how many calls?
blocks.why: Each call makes two more, and the tree only gets one level shorter on one side. With a memo it's n + 1 calls doing real work.

blocks.q: power(x, n // 2) * power(x, n // 2) instead of computing half once. What's the cost?

opts.t: O(n): the two calls double at every level, undoing the halving

blocks.why: log n levels, doubling each time: 2^(log n) = n calls. Store the result once.

blocks.q: Which is a good sign that memoization will help?

opts.t: The same arguments are passed to the function many times
The function has two base cases

blocks.why: Memoization only helps when calls repeat. Hanoi has no repeats (every call has different pegs or sizes that matter), so a memo wouldn't help it.

blocks.q: A recursion needs depth 10⁵ in Python. Best fix?

opts.t: Rewrite it as a loop that builds answers bottom-up (or keep your own explicit stack)

blocks.why: Raising the limit can crash the interpreter (the real C stack runs out). Bottom-up loops have no depth at all.

blocks.q: Explain how recursion uses the call stack, and when and how to use memoization.
blocks.a: A recursive function answers a small base case directly and otherwise calls itself on a smaller input, trusting that call to be right. Each call gets a frame on the call stack holding its arguments, locals and return point; a frame can only finish after the calls it made finish, so code before the recursive call runs on the way down and code after it runs on the way back up in reverse. Stack depth equals recursion depth, and Python allows about 1 000 frames, so very deep recursion raises RecursionError; then rewrite it bottom-up as a loop or use an explicit stack. When the same arguments recur (like fib, where the call tree has about 1.6ⁿ calls), store each answer the first time in a dict (or lru_cache) and return it on repeats: only one call per distinct argument does work, so fib becomes O(n). Halving the input (fast power) gives O(log n) calls, but only if the half result is computed once.

chapters.tagline: Put things in order once, and a pile of hard questions turns into one easy scan
goals: Explain why merge sort is O(n log n) and insertion sort is O(n²)
Sort by any rule with key= and tuples
Recognise "sort, then scan neighbours" problems
Use counting sort when the values are small
chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import Counter

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: Insertion sort is how most people sort cards in their hand: take the next card and slide it left until it fits. Merge sort is how you'd sort a huge pile with friends: split it, everyone sorts a small pile, then merge piles two at a time.

blocks.name: ds-sort
blocks.title: Insertion sort against merge sort, counting comparisons
blocks.goal: Run insertion sort to the end, then run merge sort and compare the comparison counts.
blocks.intro: In merge sort each colour block is one run being merged: the runs double in length every round.

blocks.html: Merging two sorted runs is the key move: look at the front of each, take the smaller, repeat. Each comparison places one item, so merging costs about the total length. Runs double each round, so there are log₂ n rounds: O(n log n) in all. In practice you'll call Python's sorted() (Timsort, a merge-sort cousin), but you need to know what it costs and what it gives you.

blocks.code:
people = [("ana", 31), ("bo", 25), ("cy", 31), ("di", 19)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]))            # by age
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])))   # oldest first, then by name
words = ["banana", "Apple", "fig", "cherry"]
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))
print(sorted(words, key=len))

blocks.code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
a = nums.sort()
b = sorted(nums, reverse=True)
print(a, nums, b)

blocks.q: Python's sort is stable. What does that mean?

opts.t: It never crashes on bad input
Items that compare equal keep their original order
It always takes exactly n log n steps

blocks.why: Stability lets you sort in stages: sort by name, then sort by age, and people of the same age stay alphabetical.

blocks.solution:
from functools import cmp_to_key

def largest_number(nums):
    s = [str(x) for x in nums]
    s.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: -1 if a + b > b + a else (1 if a + b < b + a else 0)))
    out = "".join(s)
    return "0" if out and out[0] == "0" else out

blocks.html: Comparison sorts can't beat n log n. But if the values are small integers (ages, grades, letters), you can count each value and write them back out in order: O(n + k) for values in range k, with no comparisons at all.

blocks.q: Explain how merge sort reaches O(n log n), and what sorting unlocks in problem solving.
blocks.a: Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item; merging costs one comparison per item placed. The halving gives log₂ n levels, each doing about n work, so O(n log n), against insertion sort's O(n²) on shuffled data (though insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted data). Python's sorted() is stable and accepts key=, so you can sort by any rule with a tuple key, negating numbers to reverse their order. Sorting unlocks: close values become neighbours (min gap, duplicates, merging intervals), two pointers and binary search become possible, sweeps over sorted starts and ends (meeting rooms), and counting inversions during the merge. When values are small integers, counting sort runs in O(n + k) with no comparisons.

Why can't it skip the answer? Say the sum is too small. R points at the biggest number still in play, so L's number plus anything left is too small too: L can't be part of any answer, and moving it loses nothing. blocks.q: Explain the two-pointer technique: its three shapes, and why the inward walk on a sorted list never misses the answer.
blocks.a: Two pointers replace a pair search over every (i, j) with a walk where each step discards something for good. Opposite ends: on a sorted list put L at the start and R at the end; if the sum is too small, L's value is too small even with the biggest remaining partner, so L can never be in an answer and moves right; if too big, R moves left. Each step drops one item, so it's O(n) with O(1) memory; fixing one number first gives 3-sum in O(n²), and the same "drop the side that can't help" idea solves container with most water (move the shorter wall). Slow and fast: fast reads every item, slow marks where the next kept item is written, so everything before slow is the answer so far (remove in place, dedupe, compress). Two lists: one pointer in each sorted list, advancing the smaller (merge, intersect, reconcile, subsequence check); merging into the same array goes from the back. Counting with two pointers adds r − l pairs at once.

sections.title: A window that only moves forward

blocks.html: "Find the longest / shortest / best contiguous stretch such that…" is a sliding window question nine times out of ten. Instead of trying every start and every end (O(n²)), keep one window [L, R]: R moves right to take in a new item, and L moves right to drop items whenever the window breaks the rule.

blocks.name: ds-window
blocks.title: Longest stretch with no repeated letter
blocks.goal: Run restart from every letter to the end, then run sliding window and compare the steps.
blocks.intro: The green bar underneath marks the best window found so far.

blocks.html:
The inner while loop looks like it makes this O(n²), but count moves instead of loops: R moves n times in total and L moves at most n times in total, because neither ever goes back. That's amortised O(n).

Two kinds of window:

KindSizeMoveExamples
Fixedalways kadd the item entering, remove the item leavingmax sum of k in a row, anagrams in a string, moving average
Variablegrows and shrinksR grows it; L shrinks it while it's brokenlongest without repeats, shortest with sum ≥ t, at most k distinct

The variable template:

blocks.code:
s = "abcabcbb"
inside, L, best = set(), 0, 0
for R, c in enumerate(s):
    while c in inside:          # window would break: shrink from the left
        inside.remove(s[L])
        L += 1
    inside.add(c)               # take in the new item
    best = max(best, R - L + 1) # the window is valid here: record it
print(best)

blocks.q: Explain the sliding window technique: fixed versus variable windows, the template, and why it's O(n).
blocks.a: A sliding window keeps one contiguous stretch [L, R] instead of trying every start and end. A fixed window of size k slides by adding the item entering and removing the item leaving, keeping a running total or count, so each step is O(1). A variable window grows by moving R to take in a new item and, while the window breaks the rule (a repeated letter, more than k distinct, sum too big), shrinks by moving L and undoing that item; then the window is valid and you record it (for "longest" after shrinking, for "shortest" inside the shrink loop while it's still valid). For counting subarrays you add R − L + 1 per R. Though there's a while inside a for, R and L each move at most n times and never go back, so it's amortised O(n). It needs the rule to be monotone: shrinking a broken window must eventually fix it, which is why sum-based windows need non-negative numbers.

blocks.html: The safest way to think about binary search: don't search for "the target"; search for the first position where a condition becomes true. On a sorted list, A[i] >= x is false, false, …, false, true, true, …, true. Binary search finds the boundary. That position is called lower_bound:

blocks.code:
def lower_bound(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)          # the answer is somewhere in [lo, hi]; hi = len(a) means "after everything"
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] < x:          # condition false at mid: the boundary is to the right
            lo = mid + 1
        else:                   # condition true at mid: the boundary is mid or to the left
            hi = mid
    return lo

blocks.q: Explain binary search as "find the first position where a condition becomes true", with the lower_bound template and its pitfalls.
blocks.a: Binary search works on any range where a yes/no condition goes false, false, …, true, true: on a sorted list, "a[i] ≥ x" has that shape. Keep the answer inside [lo, hi] with hi = len(a) (the answer can be past the end). While lo < hi, look at mid: if the condition is false there, the boundary is to the right, so lo = mid + 1; if true, mid could be the answer, so hi = mid. The loop ends with lo = hi at the first true position, after about log₂ n looks (30 for a billion). Python's bisect_left is this lower_bound and bisect_right is the first position > x; their difference counts copies. Pitfalls are off-by-ones: hi = len(a) − 1 forgets the end, hi = mid − 1 can skip the answer, and lo = mid can loop forever. The same template handles rotated lists (condition: a[i] ≤ a[−1]) and peaks (condition: a[i] > a[i+1]).

sections.title: Search the answer, not the data

blocks.html:
Some questions ask for the smallest (or largest) value that makes something possible: the slowest eating speed that finishes in time, the smallest ship that carries everything in D days, the biggest gap you can keep between cows. Finding it directly is hard. Checking one guess is easy. And the check is monotone: if a speed works, every faster speed works too.

So the guesses go ✗ ✗ ✗ … ✓ ✓ ✓, which is exactly the shape binary search finds the boundary of (chapter 9).

blocks.html:
The recipe:

  1. Write ok(x): can it be done with value x? (Usually a greedy O(n) loop.)
  2. Check it's monotone: does ok(x) imply ok(x + 1) (for "minimum") or ok(x - 1) (for "maximum")?
  3. Pick bounds where you know the answer lies: lo = something surely too small or the smallest possible, hi = something surely enough.
  4. Binary search for the first x with ok(x) true. Cost: O(check · log(range)).

blocks.q: Which phrase most strongly hints at binary search on the answer?

blocks.q: Explain binary search on the answer: when to use it, the steps, and the off-by-one traps.
blocks.a: Use it when a question asks for the minimum (or maximum) value X such that something is possible, checking one X is easy (often a greedy O(n) pass), and the check is monotone: if X works then every bigger X works (or every smaller one, for maximum). The yes/no answers over the range of X then flip exactly once, so binary search finds the boundary in about log₂(range) checks, for O(n · log range) total, even when the range is 10⁹ or 10¹⁸. Steps: write ok(x); justify bounds where lo is the smallest possible answer and hi surely works (ship capacity: max weight to total weight); then while lo < hi, take mid and set hi = mid if ok(mid) else lo = mid + 1. For "largest X that works", set lo = mid on success with mid rounded up, (lo + hi + 1) // 2, or the loop sticks. Keep checks in integers (ceil as (p + k − 1) // k; no float square roots).

chapters.title: Stacks and the monotonic stack
chapters.tagline: Last in, first out, for brackets, undo, and "what's the next bigger thing?"
goals: Use a Python list as a stack with append and pop
Match brackets and evaluate expressions with a stack
Keep a monotonic stack to find the next greater or smaller element in O(n)
Explain the "pushed once, popped once" argument
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A stack is a pile: you add to the top and take from the top. In Python it's just a list: s.append(x) pushes, s.pop() pops, s[-1] peeks. Both are O(1).

Stacks show up whenever the most recent unfinished thing must be finished first: brackets (the latest ( must close first), undo (the latest change is undone first), function calls (chapter 5's call stack), and expression evaluation.

blocks.title: A stack in three lines

blocks.html: When a new item arrives, it pops every waiting item smaller than it (it is their next greater element), then waits itself. So the waiting items are always in decreasing order: a monotonic stack. Each item is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total is O(n).

blocks.q: Why is a stack the right tool for matching brackets?

opts.t: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed

blocks.why: "Most recent unfinished thing first" is exactly last-in-first-out.

blocks.q: In a monotonic stack for "next greater element", what's true about the stack at all times?

opts.t: It's sorted increasing from bottom to top
Its values decrease (or stay equal) from bottom to top
It holds every item seen so far
It never has more than 2 items

blocks.why: Any smaller item below a bigger new one would have been popped by it.

blocks.q: The monotonic stack has a while inside a for. Its total cost is…

opts.t: O(n), because each item is pushed once and popped at most once

blocks.why: Count pushes and pops over the whole run: at most 2n.

blocks.q: Which problem is not usually a stack problem?

opts.t: Next smaller element to the left

blocks.why: That's a sliding window (chapter 8).

blocks.q: Why store indices rather than values on the stack in daily temperatures?

opts.t: The answer is a distance (i − j), and from an index you can always get the value back

blocks.why: Storing indices keeps both pieces of information.

blocks.q: Explain stacks and the monotonic stack: what problems they solve and why the monotonic stack is O(n).
blocks.a: A stack is last-in-first-out: in Python a list with append to push, pop to pop and [-1] to peek, all O(1). Use one whenever the most recent unfinished thing must be finished first: matching brackets (push openers, a closer must match the top, the stack must end empty), undo/redo (two stacks of reversible actions), evaluating postfix expressions, decoding nested strings, and simulating recursion. A monotonic stack keeps indices of items still waiting for an answer, such as their next greater element: each new item pops every waiting item smaller than it (recording itself as their answer) and then waits too, so the stack's values stay decreasing from bottom to top. Each item is pushed once and popped at most once, so despite the while inside the for it's O(n) in total. Variants: increasing stacks for next smaller element and the largest rectangle in a histogram, circular arrays by walking twice, and greedy digit removal.

chapters.title: Queues, deques and the monotonic deque
chapters.tagline: First in, first out, both ends at O(1), and the max of every window in one pass
goals: Use collections.deque as a queue (and know why list.pop(0) is slow)
Simulate processes that take turns with a queue
Keep a monotonic deque for the max or min of every sliding window
Combine prefix sums with a deque when numbers can be negative
chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import deque

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A queue is a line at a shop: join at the back, leave from the front. A deque ("deck", double-ended queue) can add and remove at both ends. Python's collections.deque does all four in O(1).

A plain list is a bad queue: list.pop(0) shifts every other item one place left, so it's O(n).

blocks.code:
import time
from collections import deque
n = 60000
a = list(range(n))
t = time.perf_counter()
while a:
    a.pop(0)
print(f"list.pop(0):     {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")
d = deque(range(n))
t = time.perf_counter()
while d:
    d.popleft()
print(f"deque.popleft(): {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")
blocks.title: list.pop(0) against deque.popleft()

blocks.code:
from collections import deque
d = deque([1, 2, 3])
d.append(4)
d.appendleft(0)
d.pop()
d.popleft()
d.rotate(1)
print(list(d))

blocks.q: Which operation is O(n) rather than O(1)?
blocks.why: Inserting or removing at the front of a list shifts everything after it. Deques are built to make both ends cheap.

blocks.name: ds-deque
blocks.title: Maximum of every window: rescanning against a monotonic deque
blocks.goal: Run rescan every window to the end, then run monotonic deque and compare.
blocks.intro: The deque (under the bars) holds candidates for the maximum, biggest at the front.

blocks.html: Two rules keep it right: a new item pops every smaller-or-equal item from the back (they're older and smaller, so they can never be a window's maximum again), and the front is dropped when its index slides out. The front is always the current maximum.

blocks.title: window_max
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 239, a hard one asked at Amazon and Google. Return the maximum of every window of k consecutive numbers, in O(n). Store indices in the deque so you can tell when the front has slid out.
blocks.tests:
assert window_max([1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], 3) == [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]
assert window_max([1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 2, 1, 6, 3, 2, 2, 4, 1, 3], 4) == [5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 4, 4, 4]
assert window_max([4], 1) == [4]
big = list(range(20000))
r, secs = timed(window_max, big, 10000)
assert r == list(range(9999, 20000)) and secs < 0.15, f"{secs:.2f}s: don't rescan each window"
hints: For each i: drop the front if it's at i - k or before; pop the back while it's ≤ the new value; append i; once i >= k - 1, the answer is a[dq[0]].
blocks.starter:
def window_max(a, k):
    return [max(a[i:i + k]) for i in range(len(a) - k + 1)]

blocks.title: shortest_sum_negatives
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 862, a hard one. Like "shortest subarray with sum ≥ k", but numbers can be negative, so the plain sliding window breaks. Use prefix sums P (chapter 4): you want the smallest j - i with P[j] - P[i] >= k. Keep a deque of indices with increasing P: pop from the front while it answers the current j (it can't do better later), and pop from the back while its P is ≥ the new one (the new one is smaller and later, so strictly better). Return -1 if there's none.

assert shortest([84, -37, 32, 40, 95], 167) == 3
assert shortest([-28, 81, -20, 28, -29], 89) == 3
hints: Build P with a leading 0. For each j: first answer from the front, then clean the back, then push j.

blocks.q: Why is collections.deque the right Python queue?

opts.t: It adds and removes at both ends in O(1); a list's front operations are O(n)
It uses less memory than a list

blocks.why: deque.popleft() is O(1); list.pop(0) shifts every item.

blocks.q: In the sliding-window-maximum deque, what order do the values have from front to back?
blocks.why: Any item smaller than a newer one is popped, so what's left decreases. The front is the max.

blocks.q: When does the front of the monotonic deque get removed?

opts.t: When its index slides out of the window

blocks.why: Bigger numbers remove from the back. Only age removes from the front.

blocks.q: Two stacks make a queue with amortised O(1) operations because…

opts.t: Each item is pushed and popped at most twice in total (once per stack)

blocks.why: Pouring can be slow once, but it's paid for by the many cheap operations before it.

blocks.q: Max of every window of k with n = 10⁵ and k = 5·10⁴. Rescanning costs about…

opts.t: 2.5·10⁹: about n − k windows of k each

blocks.why: The monotonic deque does it in about 2n operations.

blocks.title: A round-robin task scheduler
blocks.client: A home-lab tinkerer whose background jobs (backups, video transcodes, scrapes) keep starving each other on one small server
blocks.brief: Build scheduler.py that simulates jobs arriving with known run times. First, first-come-first-served with one worker: compute each job's waiting time. Then round-robin: each job runs for at most a quantum of time, then goes to the back of the queue if it isn't finished. Compare average waiting time and when each job finishes under both, on a mix of long and short jobs.
blocks.why: Operating systems, web servers and print queues all decide "who runs next" with queues. Round-robin is why one huge job can't freeze your laptop.
milestones: First-come-first-served waiting times
Round-robin with a quantum
Finish times and averages for both
A side-by-side report
stretch: Jobs arriving at different times

blocks.title: fcfs_waits
blocks.prompt: Jobs are (arrival, duration), sorted by arrival. One worker runs them in order, each to completion; a job can't start before it arrives. Return each job's waiting time (start − arrival).
hints: Track when the worker is next free. Each job starts at the later of that and its arrival.
blocks.starter:
def waits(jobs):
    return [0 for _ in jobs]
blocks.solution:
def waits(jobs):
    t, out = 0, []
    for arrive, dur in jobs:
        start = max(t, arrive)
        out.append(start - arrive)
        t = start + dur
    return out

blocks.title: round_robin
blocks.prompt: All jobs are ready at time 0: durations[i] is job i's run time. Round-robin with quantum q: take the front job, run it for min(q, remaining), and if it isn't finished put it at the back. Return each job's finish time.
blocks.tests:
assert round_robin([5, 2, 1], 2) == [8, 4, 5]
assert round_robin([3, 3], 10) == [3, 6]
assert round_robin([], 2) == []
assert round_robin([4], 1) == [4]
hints: A deque of job indices and a list of remaining times. Advance the clock by each slice; finished jobs record the clock, unfinished ones rejoin at the back.
blocks.solution:
def round_robin(durations, q):
    left = list(durations)
    finish = [0] * len(durations)
    queue, t = deque(range(len(durations))), 0
    while queue:
        i = queue.popleft()
        run = min(q, left[i])
        t += run
        left[i] -= run
        if left[i]:
            queue.append(i)
        else:
            finish[i] = t
    return finish

blocks.q: Explain queues and deques, and how the monotonic deque finds every window's maximum in O(n).
blocks.a: A queue is first-in-first-out; a deque adds and removes at both ends. Python's collections.deque does append, appendleft, pop and popleft in O(1), while list.pop(0) and insert(0, x) are O(n) because every item shifts. Queues model taking turns: rate counters that drop old times from the front, round-robin scheduling, Josephus elimination with rotate, card games, and (in Part 3) breadth-first search. Two stacks also make a queue with amortised O(1) operations. For the maximum of every window of size k, keep a deque of indices whose values decrease from front to back: each new item pops all smaller-or-equal items from the back (older and smaller, they can never be a maximum again), the front is removed when its index slides out of the window, and the front is the current maximum. Each index enters and leaves once, so O(n) for any k. Two such deques track max and min together; a deque over increasing prefix sums handles shortest subarray with sum ≥ k when numbers can be negative.

blocks.html:
A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a next pointer to the node after it; the last one points to None. You only hold the head.

Array (Python list)Linked list
Read item iO(1)O(i): walk from the head
Insert or remove at the frontO(n): everything shiftsO(1): change one pointer
Insert after a node you holdO(n)O(1)

Interviewers love lists because every trick is about not losing your grip on a node before you rewire it. Every lesson here uses build([1, 2, 3]) to make a list and to_list(head) to read one back.

head = build([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])
node, steps = head, 0
while node:
    print(node.val, "->", node.next.val if node.next else None)
    node = node.next
    steps += 1
print("walked", steps, "nodes")

blocks.title: reverse_list
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 206, the most-asked list question there is. Reverse the list and return the new head, in O(n) time and O(1) extra memory: rewire the pointers, don't copy the values into a Python list.
blocks.tests:

blocks.solution:
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev

blocks.title: reverse_between
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 92. Reverse only positions left..right (1-based) and return the head. Walk a pointer to the node before position left (a dummy helps when left is 1), then reverse the next right - left + 1 nodes and stitch both ends back.
blocks.tests:

assert to_list(reverse_between(build([5]), 1, 1)) == [5]

hints: After reversing the slice, before.next is still the old first node of the slice, which is now its last: point it at cur. Then point before at prev, the new first.
blocks.starter:
def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    return head
blocks.solution:
def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    before = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1):
        before = before.next
    prev, cur = None, before.next
    for _ in range(right - left + 1):
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    before.next.next = cur
    before.next = prev
    return dummy.next

blocks.title: reorder_list
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 143. Reorder L0 → L1 → … → Ln into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → … in place and return the head. It's three tricks in a row: find the middle, reverse the second half, then weave the two halves together.

assert to_list(reorder(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))) == [1, 5, 2, 4, 3]

hints: Cut the list after the middle (slow.next = None), reverse what came after, then alternately take one node from each half.
blocks.starter:
def reorder(head):
    return head
blocks.solution:
def reorder(head):
    if not head:
        return head
    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    prev, cur = None, slow.next
    slow.next = None
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    a, b = head, prev
    while b:
        an, bn = a.next, b.next
        a.next, b.next = b, an
        a, b = an, bn
    return head

blocks.title: add_two_numbers
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 2, a Microsoft and Amazon favourite. Two non-negative numbers are stored as lists of digits, least significant first (342 is 2 → 4 → 3). Return their sum as a list in the same form. Add digit by digit with a carry, like on paper.
blocks.tests:

blocks.solution:
def add_two(a, b):
    out = dummy = ListNode()
    carry = 0
    while a or b or carry:
        s = carry + (a.val if a else 0) + (b.val if b else 0)
        carry, d = divmod(s, 10)
        out.next = ListNode(d)
        out = out.next
        a = a.next if a else None
        b = b.next if b else None
    return dummy.next

blocks.title: A least-recently-used cache for an image service
blocks.client: A small photo-sharing site whose thumbnail server keeps re-rendering the same popular images
blocks.brief: Build lru.py: a cache with a fixed capacity. get(key) returns the value (or -1) and marks it as just used; put(key, value) stores it, and when the cache is full it evicts the least recently used key. Both must be O(1). A dict finds a node by key; a doubly linked list keeps nodes in use order (most recent at the front), so moving or removing a node is O(1) pointer surgery. Measure the hit rate on a stream of requests where a few images are popular.
blocks.why: Browsers, CDNs, databases and your CPU's cache all evict "the thing not used for longest". This is LeetCode 146, one of the most-asked interview designs at every big company.
milestones: A doubly linked list with dummy head and tail
get and put in O(1)
Eviction when full
Hit-rate statistics on a skewed request stream
stretch: A time-to-live on each entry
Compare with Python's functools.lru_cache

def stress():

blocks.q: Explain how linked-list problems are solved: reversing, dummy heads, fast and slow pointers, and the LRU cache.
blocks.a: A singly linked list is nodes with a value and a next pointer, reached from the head. Reading the i-th item is O(i), but inserting or removing next to a node you hold is O(1). The danger is losing the rest of the list when you overwrite a pointer, so save next first: reversal walks prev, cur and nxt, pointing each cur back at prev, and returns prev. A dummy node before the head removes special cases for edits at the front; return dummy.next. Fast and slow pointers solve position questions in one pass and O(1) memory: when fast (2 steps) reaches the end, slow (1 step) is at the middle; a k-node head start finds the k-th from the end; in a loop fast gains one node per step so it lands on slow, and then a pointer from the head and one from the meeting point, moving together, meet at the loop's start. Combining them handles palindromes and reordering (middle, reverse half, compare or weave), and switching lists at the end finds an intersection. An LRU cache pairs a dict from key to node with a doubly linked list in use order, so get, put and eviction of tail.prev are all O(1).

blocks.solution:
def covered(segs):
    n = len(segs)
    events = []
    for l, r in segs:
        events.append((l, 1))
        events.append((r + 1, -1))
    events.sort()
    cnt = [0] * n
    cur, prev = 0, None
    for x, d in events:
        if prev is not None and cur > 0:
            cnt[cur - 1] += x - prev
        cur += d
        prev = x
    return cnt

blocks.a: Two intervals overlap when each starts before the other ends: a.start < b.end and b.start < a.end (≤ if touching counts), and their shared part is [max of starts, min of ends]. sections.title: A tree hiding in a list

blocks.html:
A min-heap is a binary tree where every parent is ≤ its children, so the smallest item is at the top. It's stored in a plain list with no pointers: the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent is at (i - 1) // 2.

  • push: add at the end, then swap it up while it's smaller than its parent.
  • pop: take the root, move the last item to the root, then swap it down with its smaller child.

Both walk one root-to-leaf path: O(log n). Turning a whole list into a heap (heapify) is O(n).

blocks.solution:
def smallest_range(lists):
    h = [(l[0], i, 0) for i, l in enumerate(lists)]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    hi = max(l[0] for l in lists)
    best = [h[0][0], hi]
    while True:
        lo, i, j = heapq.heappop(h)
        if hi - lo < best[1] - best[0]:
            best = [lo, hi]
        if j + 1 == len(lists[i]):
            return best
        nxt = lists[i][j + 1]
        hi = max(hi, nxt)
        heapq.heappush(h, (nxt, i, j + 1))

blocks.solution:
from collections import Counter

def reorganize(s):
    h = [(-c, ch) for ch, c in Counter(s).items()]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    out, prev = [], None
    while h:
        c, ch = heapq.heappop(h)
        out.append(ch)
        if prev:
            heapq.heappush(h, prev)
        prev = (c + 1, ch) if c + 1 < 0 else None
    return "".join(out) if len(out) == len(s) else ""

blocks.q: Explain how a binary heap works and the main heap patterns: top-k, merging k sorted lists, two heaps for a median, and greedy choices.
blocks.a: A binary min-heap is a tree where each parent is ≤ its children, stored in a list with the children of i at 2i+1 and 2i+2, so the minimum is at index 0. Push appends and sifts up; pop moves the last item to the root and sifts down with the smaller child; both follow one path, O(log n), and heapify builds a heap in O(n). Python's heapq is a min-heap, so push negated values for a max-heap and use tuples like (priority, counter, item) for records and fair ties. For the k largest of a stream keep a min-heap of size k and pop when it grows past k: O(n log k) time, O(k) memory, and the root is the k-th largest. To merge k sorted lists, heap the fronts, pop the smallest and push its successor: O(n log k). A running median keeps the lower half in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap, balanced, with the median on top. Greedy algorithms that repeatedly need the cheapest or most common item, like joining the two shortest ropes, rearranging letters, scheduling by priority or Dijkstra, use a heap for that choice.

blocks.html:
A greedy algorithm builds an answer one choice at a time, always taking what looks best right now, and never undoes a choice. When it works it's usually the simplest and fastest solution there is: often just a sort and one pass.

The catch: "looks best right now" has to be the right rule, and plausible rules are often wrong.

blocks.html:
To prove a greedy rule, show that any optimal answer can be changed, one swap at a time, into the greedy answer without getting worse.

For the talks: let g be the talk that ends first, and take any best schedule. Its first talk ends no earlier than g, so swap it for g. Nothing after it clashes (g ends even sooner), and the count is the same. Repeat on the rest of the day.

To disprove a rule, one counterexample is enough. Always try to break your greedy idea with a small case before you code it.

That the problem needs dynamic programming

blocks.q: Explain what a greedy algorithm is, how you prove one with an exchange argument, and give examples where greedy works and where it fails.
blocks.a: A greedy algorithm builds the answer by repeatedly making the choice that looks best now and never undoing it, usually after sorting, so it is often O(n log n) and very short. It is only correct with the right rule. To prove a rule, use an exchange argument: take any optimal solution and show you can swap its choices one at a time for the greedy ones without making it worse, so the greedy answer is optimal too. For the most non-overlapping intervals, ending earliest is provably right while earliest start and shortest first have counterexamples. Greedy also works for reachability (track the farthest index in jump game), the gas station (restart after the tank goes negative), matching sorted items (cookies, boxers, queue order), partition labels, and with a heap of past choices for regret (drop the longest course, refuel from the biggest station passed). It fails for minimum coins with arbitrary values (1, 3, 4 for 6) and other problems that need dynamic programming, so always try small counterexamples or a brute-force check before trusting a greedy idea.

chapters.tagline: Pre, in, post and level order, and letting recursion answer for each subtree
goals: Walk a binary tree in preorder, inorder, postorder and level order

blocks.html:
A binary tree is nodes with up to two children, left and right. The top node is the root; nodes with no children are leaves. The depth of a node counts the nodes from the root down to it.

In every lesson here, build_tree([3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7]) builds a tree from its level order (row by row, left to right, None for a missing child):

`` 3 / \ 9 20 / \ 15 7 ``

Recursion visits a node and both its subtrees. The only question is when you handle the node itself:

OrderNode handledTypical use
preorderbefore its childrencopying a tree, writing it out
inorderbetween left and righta search tree in sorted order (chapter 18)
postorderafter its childrenanything that needs the children's answers first: heights, sizes, deleting

blocks.code:
root = build_tree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, None, 6])
def pre(n):  return [n.val] + pre(n.left) + pre(n.right) if n else []
def ino(n):  return ino(n.left) + [n.val] + ino(n.right) if n else []
def post(n): return post(n.left) + post(n.right) + [n.val] if n else []
print("preorder: ", pre(root))
print("inorder:  ", ino(root))
print("postorder:", post(root))
blocks.title: The three depth-first orders

blocks.code:
root = build_tree([4, 2, 6, 1, 3])
def walk(n):
    return walk(n.left) + walk(n.right) + [n.val] if n else []
print(walk(root))

blocks.q: To compute every node's subtree size, which order do you need?

opts.t: Postorder: a node's size needs its children's sizes first

blocks.why: size(node) = 1 + size(left) + size(right). The children have to be done first.

blocks.q: What's the base case for almost every recursive tree function?

blocks.q: In the diameter solution, why does the helper return the height but the answer is tracked separately?

opts.t: A path can bend at a node, but a parent can only extend one straight branch of it

blocks.why: What the parent needs (one branch) differs from the best answer at this node (both branches).

blocks.q: A tree with n nodes is just a long chain (every node has one child). What happens to recursive depth-first search?

opts.t: It recurses n deep, and Python's default limit (about 1000) can crash it

blocks.why: For deep trees, use an explicit stack or raise the recursion limit.

blocks.q: What does BFS guarantee that DFS doesn't?

opts.t: Nodes come out in order of depth, so the first match is the shallowest

blocks.why: That's why "nearest" and "fewest steps" questions use BFS.

blocks.q: Explain the ways to traverse a binary tree and how to design recursive tree solutions.
blocks.a: Depth-first traversal recurses into both subtrees and handles the node before them (preorder), between them (inorder, sorted order for a search tree) or after them (postorder, needed whenever a node's answer depends on its children's, like heights and sizes). Most tree problems are solved by asking what each subtree should return and what the empty tree returns: depth is 1 + max of the children, inverting swaps inverted children, symmetry compares outside with outside and inside with inside, and path sums pass the remaining target down. When the best answer can bend at a node, the helper returns one thing to its parent (a height or best downward path, dropping negative branches) while a nonlocal variable tracks the global best (diameter, maximum path sum); returning -1 can signal failure up the tree (balanced check). Breadth-first traversal uses a queue, takes len(q) nodes per round to get one level at a time, and finds the shallowest leaf or right-side view; the first match is the nearest. The lowest common ancestor is the first node where p and q come back from different sides, or with parent pointers the first shared node walking up. Deep chains can exceed Python's recursion limit.

blocks.q: Explain binary search trees: the ordering rule, search, insert and delete, validation, and why balance matters.
blocks.a: A binary search tree keeps, for every node, all smaller keys in its left subtree and all bigger keys in its right subtree, so inorder traversal lists the keys in sorted order and a search walks one path, going left or right after each comparison. Insert walks the same path and attaches a new leaf; delete replaces a node with one child by that child, and a node with two children takes its inorder successor's key (the leftmost node of its right subtree), which is then deleted from there. Validation must pass bounds down (lo, hi), because comparing only with children misses violations against higher ancestors. An iterative inorder walk with a stack gives the k-th smallest and an iterator; the LCA is the first node whose key lies between p and q; floor, ceiling and range sums prune whole subtrees. Every operation costs O(height): about log₂ n for a balanced tree but n for a chain, which is what sorted insertions produce. Building from a sorted list by taking the middle as the root gives a balanced tree, and self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black, B-trees) keep the height O(log n) under any sequence of operations.

blocks.q: Explain breadth-first search on grids and graphs and why it finds the fewest steps.
blocks.a: Breadth-first search starts from the source in a queue, repeatedly takes the oldest item and adds its unvisited neighbours (marking them visited when added, with distance one more). Because the queue releases nodes in order of distance, the first time a node is reached is by a shortest route, provided every move costs the same; depth-first search instead follows one path deep and returns whatever it finds first, which can be much longer. On a grid each open cell is a node with up to four (or eight) neighbours, so BFS costs O(rows × cols). To find the distance to the nearest of many sources (rotting oranges, nearest zero, nearest robot), put all sources in the queue at distance 0 and run once. Nodes can be abstract states generated on the fly: lock combinations, numbers reached by buttons, words differing by one letter. Storing each node's parent lets you rebuild the route. When moves cost 0 or 1, 0-1 BFS uses a deque, pushing free moves to the front; for general costs you need Dijkstra.

import time
import sys
from collections import defaultdict, deque
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: A graph is nodes joined by edges. Edges can be undirected (friendships, roads) or directed (follows, "must come before"). The standard way to store one is an adjacency list: for each node, the list of its neighbours. It takes O(V + E) memory.

blocks.html: Depth-first search goes as deep as it can along one route before backing up. It visits everything reachable from the start in O(V + E). Recursion is the shortest way to write it, but Python's recursion limit makes an explicit stack safer for big inputs.

blocks.title: Depth-first search with an explicit stack

blocks.html: A connected component is a group of nodes that can all reach each other. To count them: loop over every node, and each time you find one that isn't visited, that's a new component. Search from it to mark the whole piece.

blocks.title: num_islands
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 200, the most-asked graph question at Amazon. In a grid of "1" (land) and "0" (water), count the islands (land connected up, down, left, right). Every time you meet unvisited land, count one and flood-fill the whole island.
hints: Outer loops find a new island; an inner stack (or recursion) marks all of its land so it isn't counted again.
blocks.starter:
def num_islands(grid):
    return sum(row.count("1") for row in grid)

blocks.title: max_island
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 695. Return the area (number of cells) of the largest island in a grid of 0s and 1s, or 0. Same flood fill, but count the cells as you mark them.
hints: Count one for every cell you pop from the stack; compare with the best when the stack empties.
blocks.starter:
def max_island(g):
    return max((sum(row) for row in g), default=0)

blocks.title: count_components
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 323. n nodes labelled 0..n-1 and a list of undirected edges. Return the number of connected components. Build an adjacency list first; then it's islands on a graph.
blocks.tests:
assert count_components(5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4)]) == 2
assert count_components(5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]) == 1
assert count_components(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)]) == 2
assert count_components(3, []) == 3
hints: n - edges is only right when there are no cycles: the triangle 0-1-2 has 3 edges but uses only 2 of them to connect.
blocks.starter:
def count_components(n, edges):
    return n - len(edges)

blocks.title: surrounded_regions
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 130. In a board of "X" and "O", capture every region of Os that is completely surrounded by Xs (turn them into X). An O region touching the border survives. Return the new board as a list of strings. Turn it around: flood-fill from every border O to mark the survivors, then capture everything else.

assert capture(["XOX", "XOX", "XXX"]) == ["XOX", "XOX", "XXX"]

blocks.html:
Undirected: during DFS, a neighbour that's already visited and isn't the node you just came from (your parent) closes a loop.

Directed: that test gives false alarms, because two routes can reach the same node without any loop. Use three colours: white (unseen), grey (on the current path), black (finished). Only an edge into a grey node is a cycle.

blocks.name: ds-cycle
blocks.title: Is there a cycle? A visited set against three colours
blocks.goal: Run visited set only to the end, then run three colours and compare the verdicts.
blocks.intro: Every arrow points to the right, so there's no way round in a loop.

blocks.title: undirected_cycle
blocks.prompt: Does an undirected graph (n nodes, edge list, no repeated edges) contain a cycle? DFS from every unvisited node, carrying the parent; a visited neighbour other than the parent means a cycle.
blocks.tests:
assert has_cycle(3, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)])
assert not has_cycle(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)])
assert not has_cycle(5, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (3, 4)])
assert has_cycle(6, [(0, 1), (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 3)])
assert not has_cycle(1, [])
hints: A tree's edges look like a cycle from both ends unless you skip the edge back to your parent.
blocks.starter:
def has_cycle(n, edges):
    return len(edges) > 0

blocks.prompt: LeetCode 207 "Course Schedule". prereqs holds pairs (a, b): take b before a. Can you finish all n courses (no cycle)? This version treats any already-visited course as a cycle, so the diamond [(1, 0), (2, 0), (3, 1), (3, 2)] is wrongly rejected. Fix it with three colours: 0 white, 1 grey (on the current path), 2 black (done).

assert not can_finish(2, [(1, 0), (0, 1)])
assert can_finish(2, [(1, 0)])
assert not can_finish(3, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0)])
hints: Mark grey on entry and black on exit. A grey neighbour is a cycle; a black one is just finished work.

blocks.title: keys_and_rooms
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 841. Room 0 is open; rooms[i] lists the keys found in room i. Can you get into every room? It's "is everything reachable from node 0?".
blocks.tests:

blocks.html: A graph is bipartite if you can colour every node red or blue so that every edge joins different colours (two teams, no rivals on the same team). Colour the start red, its neighbours blue, theirs red… If an edge ever joins two nodes of the same colour, it's impossible: that happens exactly when there's an odd-length cycle.

blocks.title: is_bipartite
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 785, asked at Meta. g[i] lists node i's neighbours (undirected; the graph may be disconnected). Return whether it's bipartite. BFS or DFS from every uncoloured node, giving each neighbour the opposite colour.
blocks.tests:
assert not is_bipartite([[1, 2, 3], [0, 2], [0, 1, 3], [0, 2]])
assert is_bipartite([[1, 3], [0, 2], [1, 3], [0, 2]])
assert not is_bipartite([[1, 2], [0, 2], [0, 1]])
assert is_bipartite([[], [2], [1]])
hints: color[w] = 1 - color[v]. A neighbour already holding the same colour proves it's impossible.
blocks.starter:
def is_bipartite(g):
    return all(len(nb) <= 2 for nb in g)

blocks.title: bipartite_edges
blocks.prompt: Codeforces 862B "Mahmoud and Ehab and the bipartiteness". A tree with n nodes is given as an edge list. Return how many more edges you can add (no repeats, no self-loops) while keeping the graph bipartite. Colour the tree: with a red and b blue nodes, a bipartite graph has at most a · b edges, and n - 1 are already there.
hints: Nodes are numbered from 1. Count the reds; the blues are n - reds.
blocks.starter:
def more_edges(n, edges):
    return n * (n - 1) // 2 - (n - 1)

blocks.title: Bucket fill and "select similar" for a pixel-art editor
blocks.client: A teenager building a browser pixel-art editor for their friends, whose bucket tool currently freezes on big canvases
blocks.brief: Build paint.py. The canvas is a grid of colour names. The bucket tool replaces the clicked region (cells of the same colour connected up, down, left and right) with a new colour, using an explicit stack so a huge region can't overflow the recursion limit. blocks.title: bucket_fill
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 733. Return a new canvas (list of lists) where the region containing (r, c) is recoloured to new. If the clicked colour already equals new, return the canvas unchanged (otherwise a naive fill loops forever).
blocks.tests:
img = [["w", "w", "w"], ["w", "w", "b"], ["w", "b", "w"]]
assert bucket(img, 1, 1, "r") == [["r", "r", "r"], ["r", "r", "b"], ["r", "b", "w"]]
assert bucket(img, 2, 2, "w") == img
assert img[0][0] == "w", "don't change the input canvas"
big = [["w"] * 300 for _ in range(300)]
r, secs = timed(bucket, big, 0, 0, "k")
assert r[299][299] == "k"
hints: Recolouring a cell as you push it doubles as marking it visited.
blocks.starter:
def bucket(canvas, r, c, new):
    out = [row[:] for row in canvas]
    out[r][c] = new
    return out

blocks.q: Explain depth-first search on graphs and how it counts components, fills regions and detects cycles in undirected and directed graphs.
blocks.a: Store a graph as an adjacency list (O(V + E)) and explore it with depth-first search, which follows one route as deep as possible before backing up, visiting everything reachable in O(V + E); in Python an explicit stack avoids the recursion limit. Looping over all nodes and starting a new search from each unvisited one counts connected components (islands, friend groups) and finds each region's size; flood fill on a grid treats cells as nodes, and starting from the border marks regions that escape (surrounded regions). In an undirected graph, a visited neighbour that isn't the parent means a cycle. In a directed graph that test gives false alarms, because two paths can reach the same node, so use three colours: white unseen, grey on the current path, black finished; only an edge to a grey node closes a cycle (course schedule). Two-colouring with BFS or DFS tests whether a graph is bipartite, which fails exactly when there is an odd cycle.
